info.bio: Front 242 se formó en Bruselas, en el año 1981, cuando los programadores Patrick Codenys y Dirk Bergen se unieron para grabar y lanzar el disco Principles. Un año después, el programador Daniel Bressanutti (alias Daniel B. Prothese) y el vocalista Jean-Luc De Meyer se integran a la formación. El nombre de Front 242 es, según algunas explicaciones, por motivos políticos, basados en una resolución de la ONU, la 242, en la que Israel debía retirarse de los territorios ocupados de Palestina.

scenes.name: Electronic Body Music
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Bélgica acuña una de las corrientes de baile industrial más exitosas, la «electronic body music», derivada del último Cabaret Voltaire con influencia disco y de ciencia ficción: Geography de Front 242 es el disco hito; después Klinik, Neon Judgement, Vomito Negro. En Vancouver, Skinny Puppy y Front Line Assembly, profetas de la generación cyberpunk. Los cimientos de la música de baile alternativa de los noventa.

scenes.name: Industrial, EBM y The Final Cut
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: En 1989-1990 quien no escuchaba techno escuchaba industrial: Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly y los belgas Front 242 (Front by Front, 1988), con Chicago como centro americano (Ministry, Die Warzau, My Life with the Thrill Kill Kult, Wax Trax). Detroit tuvo su escena: Code Industry, el único grupo industrial enteramente afroamericano, y The Final Cut, de Jeff Mills y Tony Srock, banda de apoyo del grupo house True Faith (con Bridgett Grace) en Paragon, cuyo productor Jerry Capaldi acabó enfrentado a sus artistas y sembró desconfianza entre techno negro y blanco. Deep into the Cut (1990, Big Sex/Interfisch) cruzó EBM y techno; la última cita de Mills con ellos fue en el festival Atonal de Berlín. Srock los llevó hacia el rock (Consumed, Nettwerk, 1991).

podcast.title: Pioneering Electronic Body Music (EBM) (1981)
podcast.body: As early as 1981, Belgium's Front 242 was creating what they termed "electronic body music" (EBM), defining a new subgenre with their distinct sound and approach. "They had been creating what they called electronic body music as early as 1981."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Associated with Wax Trax
podcast.body: Front 242 was one of the bands associated with Wax Trax of Chicago, a specialist indie label for heavy music that appeared around 1990. "This was the home of Ministry Front II IV II, Front Line Assembly and Dozens More."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

podcast.title: Collaboration with Ministry
podcast.body: Several members of Front 242 contributed directly to Ministry's "groundbreaking records" during the mid-80s, assisting in Ministry's stylistic transition and highlighting a collaborative spirit within the emerging industrial scene. "Several members of Front II-IV II actually helped in Ministries' transition by appearing on those groundbreaking records of the mid-80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Final Cut
podcast.body: Front 242 was an EBM band that inspired Jeff Mills and Anthony Srock when they founded their industrial techno duo, Final Cut. "inspirándose en banda, CBM como Front II."

srcs.episode: Cómo Jeff Mills transformó el techno para siempre

podcast.title: Influence on Ministry's Al Jourgensen
podcast.body: A Front 242 show in Chicago is famously cited as the location where Al Jourgensen of Ministry had an epiphany, causing him to re-evaluate his "meek, techno pop ways" and leading to Ministry's transition into a harder industrial sound. "But legend has it that it was at a Front II-IV II show in Chicago that Alan Durgensen had as epiphany, of sorts, the one that showed him the error of his meek, techno pop ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
podcast.body: Front 242 was a key influence on Trent Reznor, specifically their "rage and fury." This inspiration helped guide Trent's evolving sound towards the more aggressive, industrial style adopted by Nine Inch Nails. "He found that he really liked the rage and fury of bands like Ministry and Front242 and Canada's Skinny Puppy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Key Artist in Spook Factory's Electronic Shift
podcast.body: Front 242 was one of the artists whose music, alongside Nitzer Ebb, exemplified the shift towards more techno and EBM sounds at Spook Factory, under the influence of DJs Fran Lenaers and Tete. This change broadened the musical appeal of the club and the Ruta, attracting a new wave of electronic and avant-garde enthusiasts. "Junto a su colaborador DJ Tete, Lenaers se inclinó a la balanza musical de la discoteca y de rebote de la ruta, a sonidos más cercanos al técno y al FM de Fran 2.4.2 o Nietzsche Rep."

srcs.episode: Cuando Valencia fue la capital mundial del Clubbing
